newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO play down peacemaking optimism.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO play down peacemaking optimism.

text.p: Israel and the PLO on Wednesday toned down optimistic notes sounded a day earlier at a meeting between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy arranged to ease a crisis in the peace process.
"Nothing was achieved yesterday," Arafat told a Brussels news conference and reiterated his frequently voiced call for Israel to implement fully interim peace deals signed since 1993.

A spokesman for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated a demand that the Palestinian Authority first take "real action" against "terrorist organisations outside the authority of the PA and inside it".

There had been few hopes before the Arafat-Levy talks, arranged in Brussels by the European Union, of any breakthrough in a peacemaking crisis touched off by the start of construction in March of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
But in the media glare of the meeting, sponsored by the Palestinian Authority's biggest financial backer, Arafat at first spoke of having achieved "significant and positive steps".

Levy, who had been largely sidelined by Netanyahu from U.S. mediation efforts, said in Brussels he was "highly satisfied" with his discussions with Arafat and sure they would be able to establish "the confidence necessary to proceed".
Less than 24 hours later, the gloss faded.
"I am looking to achieve something concrete. We are not asking for the moon," Arafat said after meeting Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke.

It was back to basics for Israel, too -- a focus on security as the top issue on an agenda of unimplemented aspects of the interim peace deals: opening air and sea ports in Gaza and a corridor for Palestinians between the West Bank and the strip.
Israel also stood firm on the occupied Golan Heights.

In the 120-seat parliament on Wednesday, legislators voted 43-40 to approve a preliminary reading of a proposed law to make the return to Syria of any part of the plateau conditional on the support of at least 80 lawmakers.
Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said cooperation with the PLO was "discussable but we need more action on terrorism".

Israel has arrested four Palestinian policemen who it alleged were involved in planning attacks against Jewish settlers. Palestinian security officials have arrested a senior PLO police officer in the West Bank.

Late on Wednesday PLO police in the West Bank town of Hebron said Israeli elite troops broke into the al-Yaacoubia school and fired several shots toward PLO police in the area. There were no injuries, they said. The army said it was checking the report.
Israel has denied Palestinian charges that soldiers recently ransacked the school and tore up four copies of the Koran there.

Bar-Illan said Israel and the PLO were likely to continue along what has been termed an informal track of discussions on the ports, passage and an official lifting of an Israeli closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

But PLO negotiator Hassan Asfour, speaking at a news conference in the West Bank town of El-Bireh, said: "There is a major political crisis and it is over the land. These contacts do not solve the crisis."

The discussions skirt the big issue of Jewish settlement on territory captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war and Netanyahu's proposal to move immediately into negotiations on a permanent peace accord with the PLO.
Senior PLO official Mahmoud Abbas (Abu Mazen), met in Jerusalem on Wednesday night with leaders of the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, a key member of Netanyahu's coalition.
Shas leader Arye Deri said participants had discussed in general terms ways to push the peace process forward, among them a future meeting between PLO officials and Shas mentor Rabbi Ovadia Yosef.
Police said militant rightist Jews were intercepted before carrying out plans to disrupt the Abu Mazen-Shas talks.
Earlier on Wednesday a Palestinian lawmaker said Jews apparently from the same group had attacked him in Jerusalem and damaged his car.
